--- title: "Multinomial logistic regression" format: html: df-print: kable toc: true number-sections: true --- # Why a multinomial model? The binary outcome used earlier distinguishes only response from non-response. Sometimes we want to look at **three or more outcome categories**, and that is the focus of this chapter. We use these categories: - `low_no_to_mild`: LSAS $< 50$; - `moderate_marked`: $50 \leq$ LSAS $< 80$; and - `severe_very_severe`: LSAS $\geq 80$. Again, we choose these for teaching the course, not because they are always the ideal thresholds in clinical settings. ::: callout-note ## Ordered categories These categories are ordered: low/no-to-mild < moderate/marked < severe/very severe. The multinomial model we show here **ignores** that order. It treats the categories as unordered labels and estimates a separate set of treatment coefficients for each non-reference category, so with two active treatment arms it has four treatment coefficients. For an ordinal outcome, the usual first choice is a proportional-odds (cumulative logit) model, which uses the ordering and estimates one set of treatment coefficients for all categories, here two [@Agresti2010Ordinal]. It achieves this by assuming that the treatment odds ratio is the same at every cut-point between categories (low versus moderate or severe, and low or moderate versus severe), an assumption worth checking. The cumulative model can be motivated by an underlying (latent) continuous severity that is cut at thresholds; here that is literally how the categories were made, from LSAS cut at 50 and 80. When the full LSAS score is available, as it is here, analyzing it directly usually beats any categorical model, for the reasons given in the [foundations chapter](logistic-intro.qmd). We use the multinomial model in this course because it is the general model for categorical outcomes, applies whether or not the categories are ordered, and makes the long-format data structure explicit. The probability-scale interpretation you learn here, how treatment redistributes probability across the categories, carries over directly to ordinal models. ::: # Long data for `mlogit` `mlogit` represents a multinomial outcome as a choice among alternatives. Each participant therefore appears once for every possible severity category. One and only one alternative is marked as the observed outcome. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(here) library(mlogit) library(marginaleffects) options( marginaleffects_print_omit = c("s.value"), marginaleffects_print_style = ifelse(interactive(), "summary", "tinytable") ) df_outcome <- read_csv2(here("data", "steps_clean.csv")) |> filter(!is.na(lsas_post), !is.na(trt)) |> mutate( severity_observed = case_when( lsas_post < 50 ~ "low_no_to_mild", lsas_post < 80 ~ "moderate_marked", .default = "severe_very_severe" ), severity_observed = factor( severity_observed, levels = c("low_no_to_mild", "moderate_marked", "severe_very_severe") ), trt = factor(trt, levels = c("waitlist", "therapist-guided", "self-guided")) ) |> select(id, trt, severity_observed) ``` ::: Now that we have the necessary columns, let's convert `df_outcome` from wide format (one row per participant) to long format (one row per response). The column `severity_alt` lists all outcome alternatives, and `choice` marks the observed outcome for each participant as `TRUE` and the two unobserved outcomes as `FALSE`. Notice how the number of rows changes between `df_outcome` and `long`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} long <- crossing( df_outcome, severity_alt = levels(df_outcome$severity_observed) ) |> mutate(choice = severity_alt == severity_observed) # one participant from each treatment group long |> filter(id %in% c(1, 3, 11)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| id|trt |severity_observed |severity_alt |choice | |--:|:----------------|:------------------|:------------------|:------| | 1|therapist-guided |moderate_marked |low_no_to_mild |FALSE | | 1|therapist-guided |moderate_marked |moderate_marked |TRUE | | 1|therapist-guided |moderate_marked |severe_very_severe |FALSE | | 3|waitlist |moderate_marked |low_no_to_mild |FALSE | | 3|waitlist |moderate_marked |moderate_marked |TRUE | | 3|waitlist |moderate_marked |severe_very_severe |FALSE | | 11|self-guided |severe_very_severe |low_no_to_mild |FALSE | | 11|self-guided |severe_very_severe |moderate_marked |FALSE | | 11|self-guided |severe_very_severe |severe_very_severe |TRUE |
::: ::: Next, we tell the `mlogit` package how to use the columns when fitting the model. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mlogit_data <- dfidx::dfidx( long, idx = c("id", "severity_alt"), choice = "choice", shape = "long", drop.index = TRUE, pkg = "mlogit" ) ``` ::: # Fit a multinomial model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mod_multinomial <- mlogit( choice ~ 1 | trt, data = mlogit_data, reflevel = "low_no_to_mild" ) summary(mod_multinomial) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: mlogit(formula = choice ~ 1 | trt, data = mlogit_data, reflevel = "low_no_to_mild", method = "nr") Frequencies of alternatives:choice low_no_to_mild moderate_marked severe_very_severe 0.25444 0.46746 0.27811 nr method 5 iterations, 0h:0m:0s g'(-H)^-1g = 1.13E-05 successive function values within tolerance limits Coefficients : Estimate Std. Error z-value Pr(>|z|) (Intercept):moderate_marked 1.50408 0.45134 3.3325 0.0008607 (Intercept):severe_very_severe 1.42712 0.45461 3.1392 0.0016939 trttherapist-guided:moderate_marked -1.41707 0.53928 -2.6277 0.0085967 trttherapist-guided:severe_very_severe -2.43872 0.61410 -3.9712 7.151e-05 trtself-guided:moderate_marked -0.87992 0.55325 -1.5905 0.1117305 trtself-guided:severe_very_severe -1.49611 0.58716 -2.5480 0.0108335 (Intercept):moderate_marked *** (Intercept):severe_very_severe ** trttherapist-guided:moderate_marked ** trttherapist-guided:severe_very_severe *** trtself-guided:moderate_marked trtself-guided:severe_very_severe * --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Log-Likelihood: -169.37 McFadden R^2: 0.05419 Likelihood ratio test : chisq = 19.409 (p.value = 0.00065319) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Store one coefficient for the calculation below b_multinomial <- coef(mod_multinomial) b_guided_moderate <- b_multinomial[["trttherapist-guided:moderate_marked"]] ``` ::: ## Interpreting the coefficients As in binary logistic regression, the coefficients are on the **log-odds scale**. With three outcome categories, the model estimates two sets of coefficients because `low_no_to_mild` is the reference category: - `moderate_marked` versus `low_no_to_mild` - `severe_very_severe` versus `low_no_to_mild` For example, the coefficient for therapist-guided treatment and `moderate_marked` is approximately -1.42. Exponentiating gives: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} exp(b_guided_moderate) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.2424244 ``` ::: ::: This gives an odds ratio of approximately 0.24. In other words, the odds of a moderate/marked rather than a low/no-to-mild outcome are lower in the therapist-guided group than in the waitlist group. More precisely, they are 0.24 times as high in the therapist-guided group as in the waitlist group. These odds ratios can become difficult to interpret because each compares **one outcome category with the reference outcome category**. We will therefore focus primarily on **model-based probabilities**, which show more directly how treatment redistributes the probability across the three severity categories. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # marginaleffects cannot recover the training data from an mlogit model, # so attach the ordinary long data frame explicitly. Supply the same data # frame, rather than mlogit_data, when requesting predictions. mod_multinomial <- set_modeldata(mod_multinomial, as.data.frame(long)) severity_probabilities <- avg_predictions( mod_multinomial, newdata = as.data.frame(long), by = "trt" ) severity_probabilities ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: And the code-block below calculates the odds ratios for the two active groups compared to waitlist, with Wald confidence intervals: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Category-versus-reference ORs for therapist-guided versus waitlist # Wald intervals on the log-odds scale, then exponentiate multinomial_log_or <- b_multinomial[ c( "trttherapist-guided:moderate_marked", "trttherapist-guided:severe_very_severe" ) ] # grab variance from the two contrasts of interest multinomial_se <- sqrt(diag(vcov(mod_multinomial)))[names(multinomial_log_or)] # exponentiate to get ORs and Wald intervals severity_or <- tibble( category = c("moderate_marked", "severe_very_severe"), estimate = exp(multinomial_log_or), conf.low = exp(multinomial_log_or - qnorm(0.975) * multinomial_se), conf.high = exp(multinomial_log_or + qnorm(0.975) * multinomial_se) ) severity_or ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|category | estimate| conf.low| conf.high| |:------------------|---------:|---------:|---------:| |moderate_marked | 0.2424244| 0.0842440| 0.6976120| |severe_very_severe | 0.0872728| 0.0261911| 0.2908061|
::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Model interpretation Compared with waitlist, therapist-guided treatment is associated with the following changes in the estimated probability of each post-treatment severity category (therapist-guided minus waitlist): - low/no-to-mild: rises by **30.4 percentage points** (95% CI **15.1** to **45.7**); - moderate/marked: falls by **2.1 percentage points** (95% CI **-20.6** to **16.3**); and - severe/very severe: falls by **28.3 percentage points** (95% CI **-44.2** to **-12.4**). The category probabilities sum to one, so the three differences sum to zero: whatever probability one category gains, the others lose. For therapist-guided treatment versus waitlist, the **OR for moderate/marked rather than low/no-to-mild severity** is **0.24** (95% CI **0.08** to **0.70**). The **OR for severe/very severe rather than low/no-to-mild severity** is **0.09** (95% CI **0.03** to **0.29**). ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} severity_probabilities |> ggplot(aes(x = trt, y = estimate, color = group, group = group)) + geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = .2)) + geom_errorbar( aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = .1, position = position_dodge(width = .2) ) + labs( title = "Estimated post-treatment severity probabilities", subtitle = "Multinomial logit; 95% confidence intervals", x = "Treatment group", y = "Estimated probability", color = "Severity category" ) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](multinomial-logit_files/figure-html/plot-multinomial-probabilities-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: # Summary - Multinomial logit models probabilities for multiple outcome categories. - `mlogit` needs a long participant-by-alternative data structure. - Interpret the model as a redistribution of outcome probabilities, not as isolated coefficient changes. - The probability differences for the categories sum to zero across any treatment contrast. - Multinomial logit ignores any ordering of the categories; for an ordinal outcome, a proportional-odds model is usually the first choice.
